title: Learning to Rank Tensor Network Contraction Plans for GPU-Accelerated Quantum Circuit Simulation
authors: Alfred M. Pastor, Maribel Castillo, Jose M. Badia
abstract: Classical simulation remains essential for developing and validating quantum algorithms, but its cost grows rapidly with circuit size. Tensor-network contraction can reduce this cost by exploiting circuit structure, although its efficiency depends strongly on the chosen contraction plan. On GPUs, plans with similar theoretical complexity may perform very differently because execution also depends on parallelism, reduction structure, memory traffic, and contraction geometry. We present a learning-to-rank framework for selecting efficient contraction plans before executing them. Each plan is represented by structural features derived directly from its sequence of pairwise contractions, and gradient-boosted rankers are trained from GPU measurements using listwise and pairwise objectives. We evaluate the resulting models on diverse circuit families, using separate in-distribution and circuit-family-shift test sets, and compare them with random and MinFill-based baselines. The learned rankers generally identify better plans, with the listwise model providing the strongest overall decision quality. We also study backend shift by comparing empirical plan orderings on two GPU architectures and evaluating the source-trained models on the second device without retraining. The rankings remain substantially, though not perfectly, stable across GPUs, and the models retain useful decision quality. These results support Learning to Rank as a practical way to reduce contraction-plan search, while showing that performance remains partly backend dependent.
summary: This paper proposes using a Learning to Rank framework to automatically select optimal contraction plans for accelerating quantum circuit simulation on GPUs. By training gradient-boosted models on structural features of the contraction plan, they achieve better performance predictions than existing heuristics. This offers a practical ML tool to manage the computational bottleneck associated with large-scale tensor network calculations.
main_problem: The core problem is selecting an efficient contraction plan for tensor network simulations of quantum circuits to minimize execution time on GPUs.
main_result: Learning-to-Rank models, particularly those trained with listwise objectives, successfully identify better contraction plans than random or heuristic baselines across different circuit families and GPU architectures.
method: The authors formulate the plan selection as a Learning to Rank (LTR) task, training gradient-boosted rankers using structural features derived from pairwise contractions.
model_or_system: The system involves simulating quantum circuits via Tensor Network (TN) contraction. The computational cost depends critically on the sequence of pairwise contractions (the plan), which is optimized for GPU execution characteristics like parallelism and memory traffic.
key_observables: Execution time measured on GPUs; ranking metrics include Top-1, Top-3 rate, regret, and win rate.
important_parameters: Contraction structural features such as bottleneck exponent ($c_{max}$), output size ($\pi$), reduction depth ($k$), and contraction geometry ($d$).
main_assumptions: The performance is strongly dependent on the target hardware (GPU architecture); the feature set aims to be portable across different software stacks.
figures_summary: Not specified by notes, but figures likely compare learned rankings against baselines and show stability/shift analysis across GPU architectures.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem of plan selection for TN contraction on GPUs. It details representing plans via structural features and applying LTR (XGBoost) with listwise objectives. Results demonstrate improved ranking quality, followed by an analysis of backend shift robustness.
why_interesting: While focused on quantum circuits, the methodology—using ML to optimize complex computational workflows based on hardware constraints—is highly relevant for simulating many-body physics problems that rely on tensor network contractions (like DMRG or PEPS simulations).
